claims.text: Controlled high-temperature annealing of Q235 steel induces a nanostructured, adherent iron-oxide scale.
The annealing-induced oxide scale acts as a protective barrier against corrosion.
The proposed barrier reduces Q235 degradation in both ambient and 700–900 °C aggressive-salt environments.
As-received Q235 steel has a native, non-optimized oxide layer.
Annealing at approximately 800 °C for 4 hours with controlled cooling promotes near-surface grain-boundary reorganization and oxidation in Q235 steel.
The protective scale is dense and spatially uniform.
The protective scale is nanostructured and comprises Fe3O4 and/or Fe2O3.
Annealing enhances atomic diffusion and rearranges the near-surface microstructure.
Near-surface rearrangement produces a stable nanostructured oxide layer that is thermodynamically robust against oxidation and salt attack.
The oxide layer limits transport of corrosive species to the underlying metal.
Limiting corrosive-species transport reduces mass change and material degradation.
Annealed Q235 samples will have a more uniform and adherent oxide scale than untreated samples.
Annealed Q235 samples will exhibit lower mass change than untreated samples.
Annealed Q235 samples will exhibit greater hardness and corrosion resistance under both room-temperature and high-temperature exposure.
The untreated Q235 native oxide is nonuniform, permits greater corrosive-agent penetration, and consequently produces higher degradation rates.
Protective behavior depends on optimization of annealing temperature, duration, and atmosphere.
Processing that causes deleterious phase formation may prevent the proposed protection.
Surface contamination or sufficiently severe environmental impurities may overwhelm or prevent formation of the protective oxide.
The composition and nanostructure of the proposed oxide depend on annealing conditions and the impurity profile of Q235 steel.
Minor alloying elements in Q235 may influence protective oxide-scale formation.
